concepts.body: A reusable named definition differs from one execution of a particular version.
concepts.detail: WorkflowTemplate owns activeVersion and inputSchema; WorkflowTemplateVersion owns spec JSON; WorkflowRun stores specSnapshot, timing, status and lineage.
concepts.title: Template ≠ run

concepts.body: A node is a graph instruction; an activity is a side-effect boundary.
concepts.detail: cond/set/terminate are interpreter control flow. step dispatches a registered capability. agent/mcp/eval/shell/containerStep have dedicated executors. Human and signal nodes wait durably.
concepts.title: Node ≠ activity

concepts.body: An agent is a versioned persona/config; a skill is prompt text; a tool executes code.
concepts.detail: AgentSkillRef orders skills. toolKeys select capabilities, and mcpConnectionId links a tool source. The implementer supports local workspace tools; generic agent nodes do not.
concepts.title: Agent ≠ skill ≠ tool

concepts.body: A connection identifies a team-owned external target; a workspace materializes its execution context.
concepts.detail: Connection.type/config/token describe integration targets. Providers are git_repo, document, issue_tracker, record and api_only. Registered types have uneven handler coverage.
concepts.title: Connection ≠ workspace

concepts.body: A stored input can be reused across executions; the acting launcher can change.
concepts.detail: RunInput.requestedById is submission history. WorkflowRun.launchedById identifies this launch; temporalRunId prevents trusting a reused workflow ID across executions. An Idempotency-Key on a work request binds to that user’s first submission and replays the run it started. A ticket’s workflow id is allocated with every row of the same repository (same host, owner and name compared case-insensitively, active or not) counted as one repository, so a run in flight on any of them conflicts; when the conflicting run belongs to another row, the response says the ticket is running without naming its workflow id. A retry or agent re-run keeps the request identity and adds an execution, which the Requests view groups under it.
concepts.title: Request ≠ launch identity

concepts.body: Spec and run-pinned settings are captured, but not every configuration read is frozen.
concepts.detail: GLOBAL agent version maps and skill revisions are pinned; more-specific agent rows resolve their current active versions. Non-run-pinned settings and credentials can change. This is selective reproducibility, not a hermetically frozen run.
concepts.title: Snapshots ≠ total immutability

concepts.body: Temporal persists execution history; PostgreSQL persists application state and searchable evidence.
concepts.detail: WorkflowRun/Step/Trace are a projection used by API/dashboard; ActiveWorkflow tracks engineering status and spend. Those records are not a replacement for Temporal history.
concepts.title: Two persistence planes

concepts.body: A policy decision records permission to proceed; another activity writes the outcome.
concepts.detail: publishOutcome returns auto/require_approval and approverCount. The template must route that result, and writeOutcome checks the latest decision. A direct runTool write is a separate path.
concepts.title: Decision ≠ side effect

concepts.body: Signals measure specific axes; passing one does not guarantee the task is correct.
concepts.detail: Online EvalResult rows include gates, review, merge, judge, trajectory, policy and PII. The offline harness compares paired golden-test outcomes and treats infrastructure errors separately.
concepts.title: Score ≠ correctness proof

concepts.body: A trusted signature proves publisher/content integrity, not safe execution or correct prompts.
concepts.detail: Install validates hash/schema and trust policy; skills and agents still require local verification. References to deployment-local MCP IDs may need rewiring.
concepts.title: Trust ≠ verification of behavior

features.body: Execute versioned JSON graphs on Temporal, including bounded loops, signals, parallel branches and human pauses.
features.detail: The shared interpreter owns graph semantics; RunnableWorkflow supplies activity dispatch, signal waits, persistence and cancellation. A graph is not necessarily acyclic.
features.title: Durable workflow graphs

features.body: Create, version, activate, import, export, compare and run reusable workflow templates.
features.detail: A template declares an input contract and workspace provider. The dashboard offers an editor and an outline view; nodes may carry optional group and title labels for display. The API validates node edges and references. Generated versions require review before activation.
features.title: Workflow library & visual authoring

features.body: Generate draft workflow specs from a description and explain existing specs.
features.detail: Generation is an activity, not arbitrary runtime code execution. Slack can draft and refine team-owned versions; a person activates them.
features.title: Natural-language workflow authoring

features.body: Agent identity, model, prompt, skills, tool keys and optional MCP connection are data.
features.detail: Template → channel → team → organization → global resolution selects the most-specific active version. GLOBAL lineage pins are frozen at run start; scoped overrides remain live. Skill text is pinned separately, by revision.
features.title: Versioned agent library

features.body: Run a launchable library agent in a throwaway repository workspace, optionally publishing a branch or draft PR.
features.detail: Separate from the engineering template. Step and wall-clock caps, admission limits and per-step accounting apply. Delivery uses a fresh trusted container. No-delivery diffs are explicitly unverified.
features.title: One-off repository agent runs

features.body: Validate context, implement with test feedback, review, fix CI failures, wait for human merge and learn.
features.detail: The default spec repeats review after CI fixes. Its CI wait can use webhook signals or active polling; human merge is an external signal, not an automatic merge. A run-pinned setting chooses whether implementer and fixer turns run the platform’s Mastra tool loop or the Claude Code harness inside the workspace; under the harness a worker-side policy decides every tool call.
features.title: Ticket-to-PR engineering

features.body: Lint, typecheck, tests, build, vulnerability scan and performance benchmark activities.
features.detail: Gate commands resolve through step configuration and repository configuration. Graph failure modes can block, warn or retry; having a registered gate does not mean every template runs it.
features.title: Configurable quality gates

features.body: Split work, execute bounded fan-out branches, aggregate outputs, merge branches and resolve conflicts.
features.detail: Branch contexts are isolated and results are structured. Cross-repo epics are separate Temporal child workflows; failed upstream repositories block downstream work.
features.title: Decomposition & parallel implementation

features.body: Enrich agent prompts with past lessons, tracker/knowledge content, Figma summaries and repository dependency context.
features.detail: The dependency graph supports manifest detection plus inference; upstream checkout is optional. Context helpers generally degrade on enrichment failures rather than blocking core implementation.
features.title: Repository & design context

features.body: Approval, decision, input form and editable review nodes pause a run until response or timeout.
features.detail: WorkflowHumanStep stores context, deadlines and response data. HumanApproval supports distinct-approver counting. Workflow status remains RUNNING while it waits.
features.title: Four human interaction types

features.body: Classify an action by risk and choose automatic publication or human approval.
features.detail: publishOutcome records a decision; templates route it to approval. writeOutcome refuses a pending required approval. This is not a universal interceptor on every external write or MCP call.
features.title: Policy-gated outcome publication

features.body: Sensitive-file, shell-command, content, diff, skill/LLM-output and PII-related scanning paths.
features.detail: A skill’s description and text are scanned in full on create, edit and bundle install, advisorily, and the result is marked incomplete if a pattern is quarantined or the scanner fails. Some checks block tool calls; others only annotate findings. Administrator regexes execute in a budgeted worker thread. Scanning is defense-in-depth, not proof that generated code is safe.
features.title: Layered runtime scanning

features.body: Run allowlisted images as shell steps or structured stdout, NDJSON or HTTP-sidecar contracts.
features.detail: Ephemeral containers default to no network, read-only root, dropped capabilities and CPU/memory/PID limits. The workspace volume is writable; opt-in egress filtering is DNS-based, not an IP firewall.
features.title: Shell & container-contract extensions

features.body: Call a named remote tool from a workflow or attach an MCP server toolset to an enabled agent.
features.detail: Generic agent nodes do not acquire local workspace tools; they may receive MCP tools. Enabling a connection type in the generic registry does not imply readSource/writeOutcome implements it.
features.title: MCP as nodes and agent tools

features.body: Let MCP clients list repositories, work requests, runs and pending human steps, and optionally submit work or cancel runs as the signed-in user.
features.detail: A stateless Streamable HTTP endpoint is an OAuth 2.1 resource server; better-auth issues tokens after a consent screen, and users can revoke connected apps. Off by default, and write scope needs a second switch. Tools reach data only through the REST routes, so route authorization applies; writes add a per-user rate limit, a budget-tier allowlist, a required idempotency key and a concurrent-run cap.
features.title: MCP server for external agents

features.body: Reply in threads, launch durable tasks, draft workflows and maintain channel memory.
features.detail: Opt-in capabilities include follow-up sessions, reactive interjections, ambient digests, passive ingestion, open-item nudges and organization signal flagging. Proactivity has cooldowns and budgets.
features.title: Channel-resident Slack assistants

features.body: Store embeddings and lessons with run/agent lineage, retrieve related items and consolidate similar memories.
features.detail: MemoryItem supports generic scopes and entities plus repo/channel/team/org links. Storage uses vector(1536); embedding model compatibility matters. Consolidation soft-deletes merged items.
features.title: Scoped semantic memory

features.body: Capture online signals, score workflow values, compare candidates to baselines and revalidate datasets.
features.detail: Hard floors are gate/assert/policy/PII. Trajectory and judge scores are soft by default; a judge call records its model and cost on the result row. A dataset run shares a runless token cap scaled by its case count and ends with a partial verdict when that cap, or its organization’s monthly USD cap, stops it after a case completed; the verdict records which, and run lists label it partial. Frozen fixture SHAs, golden tests, rubric versions and quarantined cases support reproducible comparisons. Admins can follow per-scorer daily trends, split by judge model or agent and filtered to the results of one template’s runs, and see each dataset’s quarantined share of golden cases against its ceiling.
features.title: Evaluation & regression system

features.body: Route runs between template versions and track agent canary/control outcomes.
features.detail: This is evaluation/routing metadata. It differs from the canary-rollout template, which waits for external staging and monitoring signals.
features.title: Experiments and canaries

features.body: Track tokens and catalog-priced USD across runs, runless workflows, teams, organizations and Slack channels, and stop a capped organization’s spend at launch and before each model call.
features.detail: Token tiers bind runs; a workflow with no run has a per-execution token cap. The organization USD cap is checked at launch and again before every budgeted model call, which refuses with a non-retryable BUDGET_EXCEEDED naming the organization. Both read finalized, in-flight and runless spend; the mid-run read goes through a per-organization cache of one config window. One rule, billedOrgId, places a run for the in-flight count, the mid-run guard and finalization billing: the work request’s connection, else the run’s own connection, else the repository of its own ledger row, and the first source that exists decides. A scheduled fire gets its own ledger row and run connection from its schedule’s repository, and epic planning declares the first repository’s team as its spend owner, so neither sits outside the cap. A scheduled run reaper finalizes and bills runs whose workflow ended without finalizing them. Prompt-cache reads and writes are priced at cache rates: a model’s catalog row may set read, 5-minute-write and 1-hour-write multipliers, each falling back to the code table, where Anthropic 1-hour writes cost twice input. Each trace row records its owning team and organization, which drives per-team and per-org usage reports: ADMINs see everything, a team LEAD their team, an ORG_ADMIN their organization, and the usage page opens for anyone who holds at least one of those scopes rather than by platform role. A model with no catalog price is refused on a path watched by a USD cap and otherwise recorded at zero USD with token usage retained.
features.title: Cost, budgets & usage

features.body: Inspect node attempts, tool calls, LLM responses, artifacts, policy decisions and telemetry.
features.detail: PostgreSQL is the queryable application ledger; Temporal owns durable execution history. OpenTelemetry loads as a preload so HTTP is instrumented, and trace context travels in Temporal headers, so a gateway request and every activity of the run it starts share a trace without OpenTelemetry code in the workflow isolate. A run started by a schedule has no starting context, so the workflow interceptor derives one from the workflow id and first run id and its activities share that trace. The gateway stamps its signals and updates with the caller’s context, and activities scheduled after one carry a span link to it. Trace rows link to their spec node and span; an agent’s tool calls are recorded as they execute, with real durations, and survive a generate call that later throws. Worker logs, gateway logs and the bash, MCP and harness audit lines written inside an activity export over OTLP with trace context. The run page tails new rows, reconciles by count and asks for the spec snapshot only once. Large outputs can be offloaded to PostgreSQL or S3-compatible artifacts.
features.title: Run and agent observability

features.body: Scope resources by organization/team, share repositories with teams and apply role-based permissions.
features.detail: Repository reachability combines ownership/sharing with optional host-permission checks. Per-user credentials are bound to their verified origins and the current run launcher. Query guards supplement route-specific authorization. A repository on another approved GitHub host is reached only with that host’s own credentials or the launcher’s own token, never the instance’s; with neither, the run is refused (see per-host GitHub credentials). A team’s own page also lists the repositories shared with it (sharedRepositories on GET /teams/:id), read-only, active rows only, and under an enforcing repo-access gate only those the caller’s own GitHub permission reaches; a platform ADMIN is not gated.
features.title: Organizations, teams & repository access

features.body: Filter and page the configuration audit log and runtime security events.
features.detail: Audit rows name actors by email, and a deleted actor keeps its id. Security events page on the server, with all-time per-type counts from a separate summary route. Both views are ADMIN-only.
features.title: Audit and security-event review

features.body: Launch scheduled repository work, template webhooks, GitHub event handling and maintenance sweeps.
features.detail: Temporal schedules also drive eval regression/revalidation, lesson consolidation, repository dependency scans and permission sync. Some jobs are off by default and need explicit operator configuration; provider model discovery and the run reaper, by contrast, are on by default. The schedule settings are read at gateway startup. Edits to a scheduled work request are compare-and-set on a row version and retry a few times when a competing write changed only the acting user or fire bookkeeping; any other competing change is a 409. When a repository share is removed or the repository moves, each schedule of a team left with no claim is deactivated and audited on its own (the acting user is the actor), before its Temporal schedule is paused; an audit failure is logged and does not skip the pause. The run reaper is one system-wide schedule (every 15 minutes by default) that finalizes runs whose Temporal execution is over; it is paused, not removed, when disabled. A scheduled fire is a run like any other for budgets: it gets a ledger row and run connection at its first activity, and the pull request it opens links to that execution’s own ledger row so CI signals reach the right workflow.
features.title: Scheduled automation & webhooks

features.body: The dashboard lists work by request, with the latest visible attempt standing for each, and retries a request without losing its identity.
features.detail: Run visibility is applied first, then executions are grouped by request. A single-repository request is represented by its newest visible execution; a cross-repository request summarizes every visible child and keeps failed children visible while others run. Filtering and paging happen after grouping, so an old failure cannot resurface behind a successful retry. A retry of a git request starts a new execution of the same request; connection-free and non-git requests re-run their recorded template version through the launch checks again, and an agent re-run reuses the request id with a fresh delivery branch. Optional instructions are appended to the new attempt’s description only. A cross-repository request is not retried as a whole.
features.title: Request-centred work inbox and retry

features.body: Read and write Notion pages, Zendesk comments, tracker issues and Slack messages.
features.detail: These have concrete worker connectors. HubSpot and generic http_api branches in genericActions currently return placeholders. MCP has its own executor instead.
features.title: Non-engineering API handlers

features.body: Package agents, skills, scanner patterns and templates for export/install and SDK authoring.
features.detail: Manifest v2 hashes identity and content; detached Ed25519 signatures are checked against deployment trust keys. Unverified install is denied unless allowed. Installing a skill over an existing one cuts a new revision when its text or description differs, always clears its verification, and scans it; a concurrent edit to that skill rolls back the whole install. Credentials and connection instances are not portable bundle content.
features.title: Portable signed bundles

features.body: Price models from a catalog, and on a schedule ask each provider which models it lists, storing unreviewed suggestions instead of catalog rows.
features.detail: The gateway upserts one Temporal schedule, auto-swe-model-discovery, at startup; it runs ScheduledModelDiscoveryWorkflow, a single discoverModels activity that lists models through every GLOBAL provider credential. It is on by default (MODEL_DISCOVERY_ENABLED, MODEL_DISCOVERY_CRON, read at startup); disabling pauses the schedule rather than deleting it. Results go to model_suggestions (NEW: listed but priced nowhere; RETIREMENT_CANDIDATE: a priced model missing from a complete listing) and model_discovery_provider_status, never to catalog rows, so a suggestion cannot make a model known at $0. A failed provider changes only its status row; an incomplete listing (page cap, empty result, an unfollowable continuation) still records new suggestions but deletes nothing and flags no retirement candidates; a dismissal survives refreshes; deleting a provider’s GLOBAL credential removes only the credential: the next discovery pass, scheduled or on demand, removes that provider’s suggestion and status rows, and until then the suggestions endpoint still serves them. Every failure is reduced to a fixed string (HTTP <status>, timed out, request failed (<name>, <code>; the code is omitted when absent), credential could not be decrypted, blocked address, apiBase required, unrecognised response), so no fetch or provider text reaches the status row, logs or Temporal history, and a credential save rejects a key with whitespace or control characters and an apiBase carrying a username or password. Admins read the suggestions in the Catalog tab, where the on-demand discover route refreshes the same rows. Nothing is added to the catalog or retired automatically.
features.title: Model catalog & scheduled discovery

features.body: Reach repositories on other approved GitHub hosts with that host’s own PAT or App, and never send a platform credential to a host it does not belong to.
features.detail: GitHubHostCredential holds, per approved non-instance host family, an optional PAT and/or a GitHub App (id and private key), encrypted with the platform envelope and managed by ADMINs through routes that return only whether a secret is set and its last four characters. resolvePlatformCredential returns instance, host, mismatch, misconfigured or installation-mismatch. A launcher’s own saved token still wins; a host’s set is built from its row alone (no instance PAT, App, auth mode or singleton installation) and lapses when the host leaves github.repositoryHosts. resolveGitHubToken refuses any API host outside the set’s credentialHost as a last line, for the PAT, installation tokens and the App JWT. GitHubInstallation is identified by (host, installationId) with the host fixed at creation, and a repository may point only at an installation on its own host: checked when the repository is written and again when a run token is minted (REPO_INSTALLATION_HOST_MISMATCH), The installation’s host is required wherever a token is minted: the repository types the worker’s SCM calls and the shared mint-time check take (RepoRef, InstallationScopedRepo) declare it without an optional, so a caller that does not load it fails to compile, and a repository with an installation but no host reads as a mismatch, failing closed. GitHub’s own installation lifecycle events (installation deleted, suspend and unsuspend, and installation_target renamed) are only a prompt: the gateway confirms with GET /app/installations/{id}, signed with the App JWT of the host the delivery’s secret proved, and applies only what GitHub answers (404 is deleted, suspended_at is suspended, otherwise active; a rename updates accountLogin). A host with no App credentials, a failed lookup, or an installation nobody registered changes nothing, so a forged or replayed delivery that GitHub contradicts is harmless; installations are never created automatically. GitHubInstallation.retiredReason records that a retirement came from a webhook, so a webhook reverses only its own retirements, an admin’s isActive change clears it, and the write is conditional on the row as read. Each applied change is audited with the state GitHub confirmed. The login-ownership check reads the account a login was recorded against (users.github_login_account_id) and asks that account’s host with that host’s credential; a non-github.com host with no credential is reported unverifiable, keeping the login, and a github.com account with no applicable credential is asked unauthenticated, so the check is rate-limited. A confirmed mismatch clears the login only if it and its source account are unchanged since they were read, and records a takeover. Unlinking a GitHub account clears the login only when it is the source account.
features.title: Per-host GitHub credentials & installations

features.body: A skill’s text is an immutable revision, and a run reads the revisions it pinned at start, so editing a skill mid-run does not change what a retry or replay sees.
features.detail: Every write that changes a skill’s text or description (create, edit, boot sync, bundle install) cuts a SkillRevision in the same statement, guarded on the revision number the writer read; a concurrent edit gets 409 SKILL_CHANGED (PUT also accepts expectedRevision), and the boot sync skips a race it lost. createWorkflowRun stores {skillId: revision} in WorkflowRun.skillRevisions for every skill visible to GLOBAL plus the run’s team and organization (a repo-less channel task uses its Slack channel’s). Skill reads for agents use the pinned text, and the pin is part of the resolveAgent cache key. isActive is deliberately read live (within the config cache window of about 30 s), so an admin can switch a harmful skill off under a running run. isVerified describes the current text. An admin edit or bundle install that cuts a revision clears it, and a pinned older revision never reports as verified. For custom and bundle-installed skills, only POST /platform/skills/:id/verify (ADMIN, naming the revision, 409 when stale) sets it; the boot sync re-verifies the seeded built-ins on every start, including when it cuts a revision from shipped text. Skill descriptions and text are scanned in full on create, edit and bundle install; the scan is advisory and is marked incomplete when a pattern is quarantined or the scanner fails.
features.title: Immutable skill revisions pinned per run

features.body: An ADMIN previews skills in a GitHub or GitHub Enterprise repository, then installs the chosen ones pinned to the commit that was previewed.
features.detail: Preview writes nothing: it resolves the ref to a commit and reads each SKILL.md under the path. The install request names skills and the previewed commit, never text; the server fetches again at that commit and fails with 409 if the ref has moved. A non-github.com host must be an approved repository host, and one on a private network must also be listed in a separate setting; the platform credential for that host is the only one used, and a host with none is read anonymously. Fetches are bounded in requests, bytes, skills and time. Skills with scan warnings are refused while the blocking setting is on (it is on by default). One transaction takes a name lock, checks name conflicts across the scopes the skill would be visible in, and writes the source plus every skill at revision 1, unverified, with its source commit. Markdown and text siblings are kept as reference text unscanned and nothing is executed. Wherever a model reads an imported skill’s text, it is labelled third-party with its source and short commit.
features.title: Skill import from an external GitHub repository

limits.body: HubSpot and generic HTTP API lack concrete genericActions handlers.
limits.detail: readSource/writeOutcome/runTool return ok:true with placeholder:true for several types. Notion, Zendesk, tracker and Slack have specific real handlers; MCP is executed separately.
limits.title: Some integration labels are placeholders

limits.body: A failed post-diff security gate can leave code on a remote branch.
limits.detail: executeImplementation commits/pushes first, then scans the diff and may throw SECURITY_GATE_FAILURE. Exhausted TDD iterations can also return failing tests. Do not interpret activity failure as “nothing was published.” Agent Run delivery uses a different trusted-container path.
limits.title: Engineering push happens before the critical diff gate

limits.body: The approval guard lives in writeOutcome, conditional on a recorded publish decision.
limits.detail: A run with no recorded decision is not gated by assertApprovalSatisfied. runTool, MCP and arbitrary shell paths are not covered by that helper. Template design and tool permissions remain important.
limits.title: Outcome policy is not a universal outbound-write guard

limits.body: The external call completes before the outcome-reference row is inserted.
limits.detail: A crash between remote success and local persistence can repeat a write. Concurrent invocations may race the read-before-write check. The ledger reduces duplicates but is not a transactional outbox with remote idempotency guarantees.
limits.title: Write retry ledger is best-effort, not exactly-once

limits.body: The run-start pin applies to GLOBAL lineage, not every scope.
limits.detail: fetchActiveAgent looks up active template/channel/team/org versions before applying the GLOBAL version clause. An explicit key@version is threaded through the same map, so it does not force a matching version at a more-specific scope.
limits.title: Scoped agent versions remain live

limits.body: Opt-in egress uses bridge networking, unreachable DNS and add-host entries.
limits.detail: Direct-IP traffic is not blocked by this allowlist; wildcard entries are skipped. Docker shares the host kernel, and the worker holds the daemon socket. Treat that host as a privileged trust boundary.
limits.title: DNS egress filtering is not a network firewall

limits.body: Soft scores do not automatically stop a run, and aggregate score is not the authoritative gate result.
limits.detail: decideGate blocks hard floors. judgeAdvisory:false can enable a judge threshold. The workflow still chooses which eval nodes to include and how to branch on their outputs.
limits.title: Judge scores are advisory by default

limits.body: Flake rate and judge/human kappa have configurable ceilings but nothing stores them, so only the quarantined share of golden cases is shown, as it is now.
limits.detail: The suite-health endpoint counts each dataset’s quarantined and flake-screened cases and returns the configured thresholds beside them, so its stale rate has no history. A trend filtered to a template keeps results of runs of that template, so offline harness rows, which have no run, drop out.
limits.title: Suite health stores only the stale rate

limits.body: A staging or monitoring signal reports work done elsewhere.
limits.detail: The graph waits and branches on flags, returning FAILED or TIMED_OUT when necessary. A rollback-required termination is not an actual rollback command.
limits.title: Release-gate templates do not perform deployments

limits.body: Agent Run has per-step debits; ordinary multi-step generate loops often debit at completion.
limits.detail: A model call can overshoot a checked budget before returning, and the Claude Code harness reports usage only when its turn ends. Workflows with no run have no ActiveWorkflow ledger; a per-execution token cap summed from their trace rows and this worker’s unpersisted calls bounds them instead. It cannot see calls still in flight on another worker, and a failed budget read lets the call through.
limits.title: Budget precision differs by execution path

limits.body: Launches and each later model call are refused once cached spend has reached the cap, so spend can still land after it is crossed, and some spend is outside it.
limits.detail: A call is refused only when the cached organization spend has reached the cap, so up to one cache window of spend from every run of the organization at once can land after the cap is crossed, and concurrent launches see the same total. A spend or cap read that fails lets the call through. Spend with no derivable organization is outside the cap, and a repo-less channel task bills its channel, so the organization cap never refuses it. An epic’s planning is attributed to the first repository it names even when the epic spans organizations; each child is billed to its own repository’s. An unpriced model is refused for a capped organization through a run’s ledger or a runless workflow’s spend owner; a run with no ledger row, such as a channel task, is not refused on the organization’s account.
limits.title: The organization USD cap is a gate with a one-window lag

limits.body: A run whose workflow ended without finalizing still counts as in flight until a sweep reaches it, and only while the sweep is enabled.
limits.detail: A run is looked up only after a ten-minute grace, and a sweep asks about a bounded batch, never-checked runs first, so a crowd of live runs cannot hold the batch. A failed Temporal lookup leaves the run alone, because a live run must never be billed. The schedule is set from the environment when the gateway starts and is paused when disabled, after which stranded runs count against the cap indefinitely. A run that closed long ago is ended silently, with no Slack notice, channel report or tracker update, so a first sweep over history does not post for old orphans. Reaped spend is billed to the month of finalization, so a run reaped late lands in the month it is reaped. A dashboard cancel of a run whose execution is gone leaves the run for the reaper to bill rather than ending it unbilled.
limits.title: The run reaper bounds unfinalized spend; it does not remove the window

limits.body: Team and organization breakdowns read the owner stamped on each trace row.
limits.detail: Rows older than the owner columns, spend with no derivable owner and rows written while the run lookup failed land under no team. There is no per-repository breakdown, and the platform-wide report is ADMIN-only.
limits.title: Usage is attributed when a trace is written

limits.body: A run’s trace has no workflow span, a schedule-started run’s trace hangs off a parent that was never exported, and a signal is a link rather than a parent.
limits.detail: Activities hang off the span that started the run; nothing represents the workflow or the time between activities, since that would mean running OpenTelemetry in the isolate. A schedule-started run’s activities share one derived trace whose parent span was never recorded, so a trace backend shows them under a missing parent. A signal or update context reaches only activities scheduled after it, and only the newest one is linked; work already running and earlier signals are not. The worker’s own signals are not stamped. Worker and gateway structured logs export over OTLP, and audit lines do only inside an activity; other plain console output stays on stdout. A tool call that fails input validation or names no tool never executes, so it is recorded from the step results with zero duration. HTTP instrumentation requires the --import preload, and the start scripts silence one Node deprecation code only.
limits.title: Tracing and log export have deliberate gaps

limits.body: With the claude-code runtime, the harness receives the model key inside the container the agent controls.
limits.detail: The key stays off command lines and every tool call passes the worker-side policy, but what the agent runs in that container can read it. The repository’s own Claude Code settings and hooks apply there. Only anthropic/<model> specs are supported; a credential base URL can route through a gateway.
limits.title: The Claude Code runtime puts a model key in the workspace

limits.body: An Idempotency-Key binds permanently to its first ticket, repository, description and budget tier.
limits.detail: Ledger rows are written before the Temporal start, so a same-key request during the start gets 409 IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_IN_PROGRESS. A failed stamp after a successful start, or failed compensation after a failed start, leaves the key in progress until an operator repairs the rows. Keys are never swept, and only POST /work-requests honours them.
limits.title: Work-request idempotency keys never expire

limits.body: This explorer is a source snapshot, not an operational test or security audit.
limits.detail: Routes, schemas, seed specs and tests establish implemented surfaces. No infrastructure, external credentials, LLM calls or full platform test suite were exercised for this analysis. Test presence is not a passing test result.
limits.title: Implementation is not live deployment proof

limits.body: Discovery lists ids from the keys the platform holds; it supplies no prices and judges retirement by what one key can see.
limits.detail: Discovery reads no price from a listing, so an admin still enters every number that feeds USD budgets. Only GLOBAL credentials are asked, so a model reachable through a team or organization key is not found. Listings follow a bounded number of pages and drop non-text models by a name filter; a listing past the cap, empty, or with a continuation it cannot follow is incomplete: it still records new suggestions but deletes nothing and flags no retirement candidates. A retirement flag is a hint measured against one key’s view, and an OpenAI-compatible apiBase on a private address is refused as blocked address. The schedule’s cron and enabled flag take effect only after a gateway restart.
limits.title: Model discovery finds ids, not prices

limits.body: The refresh agent reads untrusted pricing pages; the guards confine where it can write, not whether it can be wrong.
limits.detail: The workspace has network access and a shell. The path guard and checkScope keep the diff to the catalog file, the prompt treats fetched text as data, and a failed provider listing reaches the agent only as fixed words, but a hostile or misread page can still put a wrong price inside that file. The runTests gate runs in warn mode, so a failing test is recorded and the run continues to a draft PR; CI on the draft is the hard check. A run that stops because the previous refresh is still open ends SUCCESS, so a stuck schedule looks green, and the guard trusts the git binary in the container.
limits.title: The catalog refresh contains untrusted input, not prevents it

limits.body: The pull request exists, ready for review, before any person has signed off; in consensus-review it also precedes every reviewer agent (four-eyes runs its agent review loop first).
limits.detail: four-eyes and consensus-review open a non-draft pull request and run CI before their gate, so opening it can notify Slack, sync trackers and request CODEOWNERS reviewers early, and a run that ends FAILED or TIMED_OUT leaves it open. Of the built-in templates only model-catalog-refresh requests a draft pull request, and there is no step that marks a draft ready. Only these two templates guard a no-op CI fix with retryIfUnchanged; the other repush templates can still wait out a CI signal that never comes.
limits.title: Gated templates open a ready PR before the gate

limits.body: A host has at most one PAT and at most one App, and a repository on a host with neither is reachable only with a user’s own token.
limits.detail: A repository on another host with no recorded credentials fails with REPO_CREDENTIAL_HOST_MISMATCH unless its launcher saved their own token; two Apps or per-organization PATs on one host are not expressible. A login records the account it was read from, and the takeover check verifies against that account. Only a login with no recorded source (written before it was recorded) held by a user with several linked GitHub accounts is unverifiable, so no takeover is detected for it until a sign-in records one; a non-github.com host with no credential gets none either (a github.com account with no applicable credential is asked unauthenticated, so the check is rate-limited). Installations are registered only by an admin: GitHub’s events can retire, reactivate or rename a registered one, never add one.
limits.title: Host credentials are one set per host

limits.body: Skill pinning covers runs that have a WorkflowRun row, and it is not a freeze of every skill input.
limits.detail: The channel assistant’s own conversational runs have no WorkflowRun and read skills unpinned. An epic’s children are runs of their own and pin at their own start. A skill with no entry in the map, such as one created after the run began, resolves its current revision. isActive is read live, within the config cache window. A missing pinned revision row falls back to the live text, with a warning in the log and, inside an activity, a skill.pinned_revision_missing trace event, which is the swap pinning exists to prevent. A repo-less channel task finds its tenant by Slack channel id, which is unique only per workspace.
limits.title: Skill revision pins have gaps

limits.body: Grouping attempts by request reads every matching execution identity before status filtering and paging.
limits.detail: The cost therefore grows with history. A request appears once its first execution row is recorded. A retry amends only the attempt description (and the payload description when one exists), so a custom workflow that reads another input field does not see the added instructions.
limits.title: The request list groups before it paginates

limits.body: Pinning to a commit fixes what is read; it does not vouch for the author, the files kept beside the text, or the host.
limits.detail: Reference files are stored unscanned, so whatever first reads them to an agent or a person must scan them first. The host check reads address text and literal addresses and does not resolve DNS, so a listed name is trusted to mean the intended server. Commit signatures are not checked. No update check runs: the source row carries a latest-commit field and status, but nothing in the import fills them. Only imports take the name-allocation lock, so the skill API can still create a name an import has just checked.
limits.title: Skill import is pinned and bounded, not verified

limits.body: A team marked inactive keeps its members’ repository access and its shares.
limits.detail: Team membership predicates read membership rows only. Removing a repository share is what ends a shared team’s access.
limits.title: Deactivating a team does not remove repository access

usecases.body: A developer submits a repository, ticket and description, then receives reviewed code and a PR.
usecases.detail: Default path: context → TDD implementation → three-persona review → PR → CI fixes → human merge signal → memory. Other engineering templates shorten or add approval steps.
usecases.title: Implement a ticket

usecases.body: Run a library agent for an ad-hoc analysis or bounded change without designing a workflow.
usecases.detail: Delivery can be none, branch or draft_pr. No-delivery results are unverified sandbox views. Publishing validates the exported tree in a separate trusted workspace.
usecases.title: Explore or change a repository with one agent

usecases.body: Use schedules to launch repeatable repository tasks such as dependency updates or security triage.
usecases.detail: The dependency-update and security-triage templates are library content; schedule rows point at a saved template/version and target repository.
usecases.title: Recurring dependency and maintenance work

usecases.body: Plan work per repository, run independent work concurrently and respect dependency order.
usecases.detail: Epic children resolve each repository team’s default template. A failed/timed-out upstream skips downstream repositories; default-template success can require a human merge.
usecases.title: Coordinate a cross-repository epic

usecases.body: Analyze readiness, solicit clarification, decompose epics/stories, review a plan, create tickets and submit work requests.
usecases.detail: The PRD decomposition activity set differs from the simpler product-prd-draft Notion template. Tracker creation is best-effort. Story dependencies in the decomposition should not be assumed to be the epic orchestrator’s execution scheduler.
usecases.title: Turn a PRD into engineering work

usecases.body: Read a page, draft text, optionally run a brand reviewer and append/create content in Notion.
usecases.detail: Document templates route through policy checks and human approval as specified. Publishing appends blocks/text or creates a page; this is not a full collaborative document editor.
usecases.title: Draft and brand-review Notion content

usecases.body: Read a ticket, generate a response, request approval when required and post a public/private comment.
usecases.detail: record is a workspace provider abstraction. The concrete seeded support path is Zendesk; a HubSpot type label alone does not supply CRM automation.
usecases.title: Draft a Zendesk ticket reply

usecases.body: Directly create an issue or ask issueDrafter to structure a brief first.
usecases.detail: Connection config selects Jira or Linear, with a token and optional project default. Input contracts drive the run form and API validation.
usecases.title: Create tracker issues from structured input or a brief

usecases.body: Post a message to a channel from a reusable workflow with approval routing.
usecases.detail: Uses an api_only workspace and slack_workspace connection. Separate from the richer channel assistant subsystem.
usecases.title: Send governed Slack updates

usecases.body: Mention the assistant, continue a thread, ask for a durable task or draft a reusable workflow.
usecases.detail: General and code routes are mediated by workflow code; background children return structured outputs. Optional digests, open-item follow-ups and cross-channel signals expand proactivity.
usecases.title: Work with a Slack-resident teammate

usecases.body: Wait for deployment approval, staging status and production health before declaring a run successful.
usecases.detail: signal-gated-rollout and canary-rollout model gates, not deployment engines. No built-in deployment or automatic rollback is performed by these graphs.
usecases.title: Gate a release with external signals

usecases.body: Compose agents, MCP tools, conditions, human decisions and allowlisted container contracts.
usecases.detail: SDK bundles move reusable content between deployments. Custom domain behavior needs real connectors, an MCP server or a coded container capability; generic type registration is not implementation.
usecases.title: Build a custom governed automation

usecases.body: Keep auto-swe’s own built-in model price table current through a draft pull request that a person reviews.
usecases.detail: model-catalog-refresh is installed everywhere but runs only when launched or scheduled against a repository holding the catalog file, normally a fork. Before any workspace exists, the listProviderModels step fails if the file is missing and ends the run SUCCESS when the previous refresh’s branch is ahead of the default branch or has an open pull request. It then lists model ids in the worker through GLOBAL credentials, only for providers already in the file, and hands the agent text with no key. The agent edits only the catalog file: allowedPaths compares the committed tree with the session’s starting commit before the push, and checkScope re-asserts the single path before a draft PR opens. There is no CI loop or approval inside the run; the draft and its cited price sources are the human gate.
usecases.title: Refresh the built-in model catalog

usecases.body: Require two human sign-offs, or two independent review-network calls in agreement, on a change whose CI already passed.
usecases.detail: four-eyes and consensus-review open the pull request and run CI with a fix loop first (two fix attempts, a third failure fails the run); only then do two humans, or two parallel review-network calls, judge the head commit. A rejection goes to a fix, CI again with a fresh budget, and the gate again, with every round creating new pending steps. four-eyes asks the rejecting person what should change (optional, 1 h) and ends FAILED on a third rejection; consensus-review allows three consensus attempts. A fix that changes nothing never waits for a CI event: a no-op CI fix spends an attempt and a no-op review fix returns straight to the gate.
usecases.title: Two-person sign-off on green code
